name: Kettle logic
statement: Kettle logic is a defence assembled from claims that cannot all be true, offered together because any one of them alone would be enough.
meaning: The story Freud tells fixes the shape. A man is sued over a borrowed kettle returned with a hole in it. He answers that he gave it back undamaged, that the hole was there when he borrowed it, and that he never borrowed a kettle. Any one plea would clear him. Offered together they cancel, because the second admits the loan the third denies. Freud's own diagnosis is that the defendant deals with each item separately when the items have to be summed, and writes 'and' where the material allows only 'either or'. Three claims travel under the one name and are worth separating. A case can carry many arguments, it can carry weak arguments, and it can carry arguments that contradict each other. Only the third is kettle logic, and it is the one the experimental literature has left alone.

origin.note: The kettle appears in the analysis of the dream of Irma's injection, where Freud notices that his own excuses for the patient's suffering exclude one another. The third German edition of 1911 was read for this entry; a bracketed note in its opening chapter dates first publication of the book to 1900, and Freud's own cross-reference puts the kettle on page 87. He tells the story again in the book on jokes, in reversed order, with the denial of the loan first. The name is not his. Jacques Derrida writes of a plea made 'dans la logique du chaudron' in Résistances de la psychanalyse, published by Éditions Galilée in 1996, and had used the phrase earlier in Le facteur de la vérité.

evidence: No experiment on kettle logic was located, so the primary evidence is a pair of passages. In the 1911 German edition Freud writes that his explanations for Irma's illness 'stimmen untereinander nicht zusammen, ja sie schließen einander aus', and that the whole plea recalls the defence of a man accused by his neighbour of giving back a kettle in a damaged state: 'Erstens habe er ihn unversehrt zurückgebracht, zweitens war der Kessel schon durchlöchert, wie er ihn entlehnte, drittens hatte er nie einen Kessel vom Nachbar entlehnt.' Brill's 1913 translation carries the three pleas in that order and adds that if even one is recognised as valid the man must be acquitted. Brill's 1916 translation of the joke book prints the story with the order reversed, as a copper kettle and a lawsuit, the defence opening 'In the first place I never borrowed any kettle from B.' Freud calls it a sophism whose nucleus is an omission, writes that each separate protest is good by itself while together they exclude each other, and says the defendant treats individually what must be taken as a whole. Later in the same book he doubts it is a joke at all and grants that it is far more correct to call the kettle story comic than witty. Derrida is the vector for the name. He glosses the plea as three moves: the kettle he returns is intact, the holes were already in it, and no kettle was ever lent. The nearest experiments manipulate something else. Petty and Cacioppo ran a pilot on 46 undergraduates who read a message favouring a tuition rise at their own university or at a distant one, carrying three cogent arguments, three specious ones, or the three cogent followed by the three specious. Message type mattered, F(2, 40) = 11.27, p < .001, and interacted with involvement, F(2, 40) = 2.72, p < .07. Where the rise was distant, the six-argument message drew more agreement than either three-argument message, ps < .05, and three cogent arguments did not beat three specious ones. Where the rise was their own, three cogent arguments beat three specious ones, p < .05, and adding the three specious ones bought nothing. Their full experiment gave 168 Missouri undergraduates three or nine arguments, all cogent or all specious, at high or low involvement, and summed four 9-point scales into an attitude score. Strong arguments beat weak overall, 8.30 against 4.34, F(1, 158) = 18.74, p < .0001. Number mattered more at low involvement, F(1, 158) = 3.98, p < .05, with a simple effect of F(1, 158) = 9.12, p < .01 there and F < 1 at high involvement. Quality mattered more at high involvement, F(1, 158) = 13.04, p < .0004, with F(1, 158) = 32.87, p < .0001 there and F < 1 at low involvement. Inside the high-involvement half, number crossed with quality, F(1, 79) = 6.11, p < .02, and the attitude means show why: three weak arguments scored 4.10 and nine weak scored 1.05, while three strong scored 8.32 and nine strong scored 11.30. Padding a good case with bad arguments cost the case something once the audience was paying attention.

replication.headline: No experiment presenting mutually inconsistent arguments and measuring what they do to an audience was found. The searchable literature manipulates how many arguments there are and how good they are, which are different claims.
replication.detail: The closest modern work is Obermaier and Koch, who ran four experiments in German on whether weak arguments add to a strong one or average it down. In Study 1a, 156 people read a politician's post about renovating a cultural centre. Three weak arguments plus the strong one drew more support, n = 50, M = 4.22, SD = 0.71, than the strong argument alone, n = 50, M = 3.88, SD = 0.79, or the weak three alone, n = 53, M = 3.49, SD = 0.93, F(2, 150) = 10.47, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.12, tested one-tailed. Study 1b changed the topic to a railway and reversed the result: the strong argument alone did best, n = 57, M = 3.75, SD = 0.90, ahead of the strong argument with three weak ones, n = 58, M = 3.47, SD = 0.79, and the weak three alone, n = 57, M = 2.70, SD = 0.94, F(2, 169) = 21.78, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.21. Study 2 put one strong argument for a swimming pool renovation against that argument plus four weak ones, and the padded version did worse, 4.04 against 4.32, t(116) = 2.11, p = .02, d = 0.39. Study 3 split the difference on purpose. A strong argument for a health check scored 3.56 alone, fell to 3.11 with three clearly weak additions, and rose to 4.07 with three additions of moderate strength, F(2, 120) = 9.33, p = .001, partial eta squared 0.14. Their reading is that padding helps when the extra arguments are merely less good and hurts when they are plainly bad. Bergman, Hussein, Catapano and Tormala report from the other side of the same question that many arguments make a source look more expert and also look more intent on persuading, and that the two perceptions suppress each other, leaving little net gain. That description is taken from their abstract at Crossref rather than from the article. None of these studies makes its arguments contradict one another, which is the move the name is about. The dilution effect is the other neighbour, and it has its own entry in this corpus at number 405. Highhouse and colleagues ran a preregistered replication of the basic dilution effect on 796 participants predicting a student's grade point average, and their abstract reports no evidence for dilution despite an unusually large sample and a strong manipulation. Inconsistency has been modelled formally rather than tested. Timotheus Kampik defines kettle logic as an agent advancing inconsistent arguments to defeat a claim, and his abstract reports that every abstract argumentation semantics he analysed suffers from it, naive semantics excepted, so a formal reasoner can be moved by an inconsistent set that a consistent subset would not move as far. That is a theorem about inference functions and not a measurement of people. Searches for a human experiment covered Europe PMC phrase queries for kettle logic, self-contradictory arguments, mutually inconsistent arguments and contradictory arguments in persuasion, Crossref bibliographic queries on kettle logic and on argument number and inconsistency, and general web search. The five Europe PMC records for the phrase are criminology, policy and history commentary, and one of them is about police kettling rather than about Freud.

limits: The concept is a label for a rhetorical move, and it does not say which way the move cuts. Freud's defendant is a joke figure whose pleas are absurd, and the courts take the opposite view of the same structure. Rule 8(d)(2) of the United States Federal Rules of Civil Procedure lets a party 'set out 2 or more statements of a claim or defense alternatively or hypothetically', and provides that the pleading is sufficient if any one of them is sufficient, while Rule 8(d)(3) permits as many separate claims or defences 'regardless of consistency'. Several things could not be obtained. Reich and Tormala's 2013 paper on contradictions and persuasion is paywalled and no abstract for it was served by Crossref or Semantic Scholar, so nothing is claimed here about what it found. Kampik's article was located as open access at two addresses, and both returned a challenge page rather than the file, so it is described from its Crossref abstract alone. Bergman and colleagues were read the same way. Nisbett, Zukier and Lemley's original dilution paper was not obtained here either; the repository copy answered with a bot challenge. The Petty and Cacioppo article is a scan without a text layer and was read by optical recognition run twice at different resolutions, with the attitude means checked in both passes. The first German edition of the book on jokes was not obtained, and no publication year is asserted for it. The English versions used are Brill's, which are the free ones, not the Standard Edition, and translators differ over the wording.
misreadings: The commonest error is to file the two Freud versions under one citation. The dream book gives the pleas as returned undamaged, already holed, never borrowed. The joke book reverses that, opening with the denial that any kettle was borrowed, and adds the copper and the lawsuit that most retellings carry. A reader quoting 'Freud's kettle' is usually quoting the second while citing the first. The second error is to treat Freud as making a point about arguing. He is describing dreams, and the kettle is his evidence that unconscious material sets contradictory thoughts side by side without an 'either or'. He was unsure the story was even a joke. The third error is to read the dilution effect as a test of this fallacy. Dilution is about non-diagnostic detail making a judgement less extreme, its own replication record is unsettled, and nothing in it involves claims that contradict one another. The fourth is to assume the fallacy has been measured because the neighbouring effects have. Weak arguments and incompatible arguments are separate manipulations, and the experiments located here vary only the first. The last error is to treat every multi-part defence as kettle logic. Legal systems allow alternative and inconsistent pleading on purpose, because a party often does not know which version of the facts a court will find, and the fallacy is in asserting all the versions at once as true rather than in offering them as alternatives.

sources.text: Freud, S. (1911). Die Traumdeutung. Dritte vermehrte Auflage. Leipzig and Vienna: Franz Deuticke. The German wording quoted here was read in the scanned text of this edition; the same document dates the book's first publication to 1900.
Freud, S. (1913). The Interpretation of Dreams. Translated by A. A. Brill. New York: Macmillan. Chapter 2 was read in full for the kettle passage.

Freud, S. (1916). Wit and Its Relation to the Unconscious. Translated by A. A. Brill. New York: Moffat, Yard and Company. Read in full text; the kettle story and Freud's later doubt about whether it is a joke were both taken from it.

Derrida, J. (1996). Résistances de la psychanalyse. Paris: Éditions Galilée. The phrase 'la logique du chaudron' and its three-part gloss were read in the French text, and the same passage was checked against the 1998 Stanford University Press translation by Peggy Kamuf, Pascale-Anne Brault and Michael Naas.

Petty, R. E., & Cacioppo, J. T. (1984). The effects of involvement on responses to argument quantity and quality: Central and peripheral routes to persuasion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 46(1), 69-81. Every figure quoted here was read off the scanned article.

Obermaier, M., & Koch, T. (2024). The paradox of argument strength: how weak arguments undermine the persuasive effects of strong arguments. Scientific Reports, 14, 22244. Open access, read in full as the JATS XML.

Bergman, A., Hussein, M. A., Catapano, R., & Tormala, Z. L. (2025). Fifteen reasons you should read this paper: How providing many arguments increases perceptions of both expertise and persuasive intent. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Described here from the abstract served by Crossref.

Kampik, T. (2023). Kettle logic in abstract argumentation. Journal of Logic and Computation, 34(3), 528-556. Described from the abstract served by Crossref; two open-access addresses for the file returned challenge pages.

Highhouse, S., Freier, L. M., Stevenor, B. A., Shea, M. A., Childers, M., & Melick, S. R. (2022). Failure to replicate the basic dilution effect in performance prediction. International Journal of Selection and Assessment, 30(2), 195-201. Read as the abstract served by Crossref, which is the source of the sample size and of the finding.

Nisbett, R. E., Zukier, H., & Lemley, R. E. (1981). The dilution effect: Nondiagnostic information weakens the implications of diagnostic information. Cognitive Psychology, 13(2), 248-277. Named as the origin of the neighbouring effect; not obtained, and no figure from it appears here.

Reich, T., & Tormala, Z. L. (2013). When contradictions foster persuasion: An attributional perspective. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 49(3), 426-439. Located during the search for tests of inconsistency; paywalled, no abstract served, and nothing is claimed here about its contents.
Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule 8(d). Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School. The quoted wording of subdivisions (d)(2) and (d)(3) was read here.
